physics.scenario: An electric immersion heater warms 0.400 kg of water in an uninsulated glass beaker with no lid. The p.d. and current are constant. The water is stirred and a digital thermometer is read every 150 s for 900 s.
principles: Electrical power P = VI (B.5); energy supplied E = VIt
Q = mcΔT for the energy that stays in the water (B.1)
Energy is lost from the beaker to the surroundings at a rate that increases with the temperature excess (conduction, convection, evaporation)
assumptions: The rate of energy loss is h(θ − θ_r) with a constant h (Newton's law of cooling, an empirical model)
The beaker, heater and thermometer have negligible heat capacity
The water starts at room temperature θ_r
derivation: Solution with θ = θ_r at t = 0: θ = θ_r + (P/h)(1 − e^(−ht/(mc)))
The rate dθ/dt = (P/mc)e^(−ht/(mc)) falls as the water warms, so ΔT is less than Pt/(mc) and c = VIt/(mΔT) is too large
Near t = 0 the loss is small, so the early rate of rise gives c closest to the true value

h.note: loss coefficient of an open, uninsulated beaker (about 8 W lost at 20 K above the room)

heating-with-loss.statement: θ = θ_r + (P/h)(1 − e^(−ht/(mc))), from mc dθ/dt = P − h(θ − θ_r) with θ = θ_r at t = 0 (an empirical loss model, Newton's law of cooling, beyond the syllabus; it reduces to θ = θ_r + Pt/(mc) when h → 0)
heating-with-loss.f: ({ thetaR, P, h, m, c, t }) => (h === 0 ? thetaR + (P * t) / (m * c) : thetaR + (P / h) * -Math.expm1((-h * t) / (m * c)))

text.stem: A student determines the specific heat capacity $c$ of water. An electric immersion heater is placed in $(0.400 \pm 0.001)\ \text{kg}$ of water in a glass beaker with no lid and no insulation. The p.d. across the heater is $V = (12.0 \pm 0.1)\ \text{V}$ and the current in it is $I = (3.50 \pm 0.05)\ \text{A}$; both stay constant. The heater is switched on at $t = 0$ and the stirred water's temperature $\theta$ is recorded. Times are measured to $\pm 1\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Use the data to show that the rate at which the temperature of the water rises decreases during the heating.
markscheme: In the first 150 s the temperature rises by 3.7 °C ✓
In the last 150 s it rises by only 3.1 °C, although the energy supplied in each interval is the same ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate $c$ using the readings at $t = 0$ and $t = 900\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: c
parts.question: The accepted value of $c$ for water is $4180\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. Explain, with reference to your answer to (a), why the value in (b) is larger than the accepted value.
markscheme: The falling rate of rise shows that energy is lost to the surroundings, at a greater rate as the water gets hotter ✓
So less than $VIt$ goes into the water and $\Delta T$ is smaller than it would be with no losses; $c = \dfrac{VIt}{m\Delta T}$ is therefore too large ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate $c$ using only the first 150 s of heating.

parts.label: e
parts.question: Explain why using only the first 150 s reduces the effect of the energy losses.
markscheme: At the start the water is close to room temperature, so the rate of energy loss is small and almost all of $VIt$ goes into the water ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: The uncertainty in the value from (b) is about $\pm 170\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ and in the value from (d) about $\pm 370\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. Discuss which value is the better estimate of $c$.
markscheme: (b) is more precise (smaller uncertainty), but its range, about 4490 to 4820, does not include 4180: it has a systematic error ✓

(d) has a larger uncertainty (small $\Delta T$), but its range, about 3890 to 4620, includes 4180: it is more accurate, so (d) is the better estimate (award for a conclusion consistent with the candidate's own values) ✓
